edits.before: An increase in the money supply generally leads to an increase in overall economic activity/value in the economy. There is an inverse relationship between interest rate and demand for money.
edits.after: More money supply does not guarantee an equal increase in real output: effects depend on prices, interest rates, expectations and capacity. A higher market interest rate tends to reduce desired money balances by raising the opportunity cost of holding money.

edits.before: Perfectly Elastic (infinite response to any price change) vs Perfectly Inelastic (zero response) are opposite extremes — commonly reversed in tricky MCQs.
edits.after: Perfectly elastic = horizontal curve (infinite elasticity); perfectly inelastic = vertical curve (zero elasticity). For ordinary demand, Ep is negative and is often reported in absolute value.

edits.before: Monopoly has complete price control while Oligopoly has interdependent pricing among a few firms — don't confuse "one seller" with "few sellers."
edits.after: Monopoly = one seller, a price maker constrained by market demand. Oligopoly = a few dominant firms with strategically interdependent decisions.

edits.before: Economics is the Science of Wealth — how society allocates scarce resources (land, labour, capital) to produce output (goods and services).
edits.after: The classical wealth-oriented view is associated with Adam Smith. Modern economics studies choice under scarcity, resource allocation, production, distribution, consumption and welfare.

edits.before: Adam Smith = Father of Economics (1776 book); Alfred Marshall = Father of Demand-Supply theory (1890 book) — don't mix these two "firsts."
edits.after: Adam Smith = Father of Economics; Wealth of Nations (1776). Alfred Marshall = influential systematic treatment of demand, supply and equilibrium in Principles of Economics (1890).

edits.before: Elasticity of Demand: Change in quantity demanded due to change in price (or income, or price of related goods).
edits.after: Elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to changes in own price, income or the price of a related good.

edits.before: Law of Supply shows a positive relationship between price and supply, assuming other factors remain constant
edits.after: Law of Supply: Own price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, ceteris paribus; an own-price change causes movement along the supply curve

edits.before: Demand for a commodity = Desire + Willingness to buy + Ability to Purchase, for Satisfaction (Utility)
edits.after: Effective demand = Desire + Willingness + Ability to buy a quantity at a given price and time

edits.before: There exists an inverse relationship between price and demand, assuming other factors remain constant.
edits.after: Own price and quantity demanded are inversely related, ceteris paribus; an own-price change causes movement along the same demand curve.

edits.before: Supply: Quantity of goods that a producer is willing to sell at different prices at a given time.
edits.after: Supply: Quantities producers are willing and able to offer at various prices during a given period, other things equal.

edits.before: Socialism ≠ Communism in strict economic classification — this chapter defines Socialist Economy via Karl Marx's concept with state ownership, distinct from the Mixed Economy model India follows.
edits.after: Market-oriented systems emphasize decentralized private decisions; command systems emphasize central public control; mixed economies combine market and government roles. Socialist ideas predated Marx.

edits.before: As a country develops, sector GDP contribution generally follows: Agriculture < Industry < Services. India already fits this pattern with Services contributing the highest share (~55%).
edits.after: Development often reduces agriculture's relative share, though paths differ. India's nominal GVA shares in FY 2025–26 PE: Services ~54.3% > Secondary ~25.8% > Primary ~19.9%. Collar labels are not official sector definitions.

edits.before: India ranks 4th by nominal GDP but 3rd by PPP — the PPP ranking adjusts for cost-of-living differences, pushing India ahead of Germany and Japan.

edits.before: India is classified as a Mixed Economy, based on the Gandhian Principle of Trusteeship for balancing private ownership with social welfare.
edits.after: India is a mixed, increasingly market-oriented economy. Its model evolved through public-private coexistence, planning, regulation and post-1991 reforms; trusteeship is a separate normative idea.
